children.text: A National Shrine that recreates, on its original site, the house where Filipino national hero Jose Rizal was born on

. Inside this Spanish colonial-era stone house, his childhood belongings and his family's living spaces have been re-created, and since there's no admission fee, it makes for an easy history outing just outside Manila.
Rizal Shrine Calamba is the house where Jose Rizal, the spiritual leader of the Philippine independence movement, was born on
and spent his childhood. It stands about
55km

south of Manila, at the corner of Francisco Mercado Street and Jose P. Rizal Street in Calamba's old town (Poblacion), right next to San Juan Bautista (St. John the Baptist) Church, where Rizal was baptized. It's run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) as the "Museo ni Jose Rizal" and is designated a Level 1 National Shrine. The grounds cover about 3,704 square meters, and six galleries display photographs, replicas, and belongings.

The original house was a two-story "bahay na bato" built over about two years by Rizal's father, Francisco Mercado. It was a classic mansion of the Spanish colonial-era elite, with a ground floor of adobe stone and brick, an upper floor of solid wood, and sliding windows fitted with capiz shells. Rizal was the seventh of eleven children. The family leased farmland owned by the Dominican order, but after a dispute over rent they were evicted, and the house was seized by Spanish authorities in

. This episode is counted among the reasons Rizal came to write his critiques of the colonial system. In this house the young Rizal learned his letters from his mother, Teodora, at around age three, and studied Latin and arithmetic with a private tutor brought into the home. The death of his beloved younger sister Concepcion at age three in
is counted as the first great sorrow he experienced, and he grew up among the Calamba fields and beside Laguna Lake until he left for school in Biñan at age nine, in
The house was destroyed during World War II and eventually torn down, and the government bought the remaining lot for
. On

, President Elpidio Quirino allowed a student fundraising drive through Executive Order No. 145. Coins collected at 5 centavos per elementary student, 10 centavos per high school student, and 20 centavos per college student covered a large share of the rebuilding cost, and under the supervision of architect Juan Nakpil, using the original materials and construction methods of the period, the house opened on Rizal's birthday,
. Only the original flooring and the well, which were found during the reconstruction, remain exactly as they were.
In
a building with galleries, a library, a video room, and a gift shop was added alongside, and in
the exterior was repainted green to match the meaning of Rizal's surname, "green fields" (ricial), which stirred some controversy over the color.
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
is enough to see everything. Combined with
Rizal Park
and
Fort Santiago
in Manila, it completes a journey that follows Rizal's life from the house where he was born to the place of his execution.

blocks.title: The room where Rizal was born

children.text: A four-poster bed stands in the largest master bedroom on the second floor. This room, where Rizal was born, connects to the children's rooms (the one shared by Rizal and his older brother Paciano, and the one used by his nine older and younger sisters), so you can picture the daily life of a large family.

The stone ground floor, once the stables and storeroom, holds Galleries 1 to 3. Following the family roots, childhood, and schooling, you can see a copy of the baptismal certificate and replicas of his childhood writings and drawings.

blocks.title: Touring the bahay na bato home

children.text: The living room where guests were received, the formal dining room and study, the family dining room with the large fan called a "punkah," the kitchen, and the veranda "azotea" all preserve the layout of an upper-class household. The study, with more than 1,000 books, is said to have been the largest in Calamba at the time.

blocks.title: Young Rizal with his dog, and the bahay kubo

children.text: The garden holds a bronze statue of young Rizal and his dog, erected in
for the 100th anniversary of Rizal's execution. Together with the bahay kubo modeled on the hut where young Rizal played and carved, it's a great spot for a family photo.

blocks.title: His parents' graves and the old well

children.text: The garden holds the graves of his father Francisco and his mother Teodora. Their remains had been in the Manila North Cemetery and were moved here in the 1990s. The well beside the kitchen is one of the few original remains and is now called the wishing well.

blocks.title: San Juan Bautista Church, where he was baptized

children.text: The church beside the birth house is where Rizal was baptized on
. A fire in
burned the old baptismal records, which were restored from handwritten copies, and the baptistery was designated a National Historical Landmark in
. You can see the restored baptismal font, a handwritten copy of the certificate, and stained glass depicting St. Dominic and San Lorenzo Ruiz.

blocks.title: The giant Rizal monument in front of city hall

children.text: Unveiled by President Aquino on
, the 150th anniversary of his birth, this bronze statue stands about
tall. Its height stands for the 22 languages Rizal mastered, and the 15-step staircase stands for the 150th anniversary.
The giant jar sculpture in the plaza depicts the story behind the name Calamba, and the names of the city's barangays are inscribed on its surface. It's a few minutes' walk from the birth house.
Depart Manila by bus to Calamba, or by car
Arrive when the museum opens and tour the family and childhood exhibits in Galleries 1 to 3 on the ground floor
Walk through the second-floor living room, bedrooms, dining room, kitchen, and azotea, and see the master bedroom where Rizal was born
See the young Rizal statue, the bahay kubo, and his parents' graves in the garden
See the exhibits on Rizal's European travels and novel writing in Galleries 5 and 6 of the annex
See the baptismal font and the handwritten copy of the certificate at San Juan Bautista Church
Take photos of the Calambanga jar in the plaza, and have lunch at a restaurant in town
Take a tricycle to the Rizal monument in front of city hall and the Calamba Baywalk and back
Return to the bus terminal and head back to Manila or on to your next destination

The birth house, the church, and Calambanga are clustered in one area, so you can get around on foot. If it rains, do the indoor exhibits first and skip the monument in front of city hall and the Baywalk. If your schedule is tight, enter the shrine before
3 p.m.
so that you can see Galleries 5 and 6 of the annex before they close.

items.title: Full-day extended route
items.subtitle: Shrine + hot springs or Los Baños

children.text: Visit the Rizal Shrine, the church, and Calambanga (same as the half-day route)
Head toward Pansol for lunch
Relax at a Pansol hot-spring resort pool, or stroll the University of the Philippines Los Baños campus and the foot of Mount Makiling
Buy some buko pie in Los Baños and head back to Manila
The museum closes at
4 p.m.
Tuesday through Sunday and is closed on Mondays, so it's safer to visit the shrine first in the morning and schedule the hot springs afterward.

From Pasay Buendia, One Ayala in Makati, PITX, and Cubao, take a bus bound for Calamba, Santa Cruz, or Los Baños (JAC Liner, Jam Liner, Saint Rose, and others) and get off at Calamba Crossing or the Turbina terminal. It takes
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
depending on traffic, for a one-way fare of about
. Published fares run about
on a Jam Liner from PITX and about
from Buendia, varying with the bus class.
On the way back, take a Jam Liner toward Cubao or a bus toward Buendia from the Crossing. Several operators are said to run at roughly one-hour intervals, but check the last bus time on site.
From the Crossing to the old town where the shrine stands is about
, reachable by jeepney or tricycle in
10–15 minutes
From Manila, take SLEX south for about
55km
and exit at Calamba. Without traffic it takes
45 minutes–1 hour
, though on weekend afternoons and holidays congestion is heavy and the trip can take up to twice as long. The Alabang–Calamba toll for a passenger car (Class 1) has been
since
July 1, 2026
, paid with an Autosweep RFID. The road in front of the shrine is a narrow one-way street, so park along Jose P. Rizal Street or use a parking lot near the church. A Grab from Makati runs about
one way, but this varies a lot by time of day. From the airport (NAIA), it takes around 1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes via SLEX.
The Alabang–Calamba section of the PNR commuter line stopped running on
July 2, 2023
for North-South Commuter Railway (NSCR) construction, and the Tutuban–Alabang section has also been closed since
March 28, 2024
. No reopening date has been announced, so use a bus or a car.
The shrine, the church, and Calambanga are all just a few minutes' walk from each other. The Rizal monument in front of city hall is about
2km
from the shrine, and chartering a tricycle to take in the Baywalk as well starts at about
, while short tricycle rides within town start at about
Since it's an indoor museum, you can visit year-round regardless of weather. If you plan to walk the garden and the plaza too, the drier
November–April
season is more comfortable, and in
March–May
, when midday temperatures climb to
, a morning visit is recommended. During the
June–October
rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, and low-lying roads along Laguna Lake can flood during typhoons.
On Rizal's birthday,
June 19
, the shrine holds a commemorative ceremony and wreath-laying, making it the busiest day. In
as well, for the 165th anniversary, there was a ceremony attended by senators and the Laguna governor, among others. Rizal Day (
December 30

), the national holiday marking the day of his execution, also brings memorial events. On event days, visits may be restricted or hours changed, so check the museum's official Facebook page for the latest notices.

On weekday mornings during the school term, student groups on field trips are common. If you'd rather visit quietly, aim for a weekday afternoon or right after opening on a weekend. The garden and plaza have little shade and are hot at midday, and the Baywalk offers a clear view of Laguna Lake and Mount Makiling only when the sky is clear.

Pansol hot-spring resort
items.note: Big gap between weekday and weekend rates, check before booking

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
A day trip from Manila is plenty, but if you're continuing a Laguna trip, staying in Calamba is also a good option. Business hotels around Calamba Crossing and the large malls run about

per night, while the Pansol area at the foot of Mount Makiling clusters private resorts that draw on hot-spring water — many families rent a whole private-pool villa. Weekend rates run considerably higher than weekdays, so compare in advance, and a weekday visit is much quieter.

The old town around the shrine has a few simple Filipino restaurants and cafes, and franchise restaurants cluster around Calamba Crossing and the malls, so the choice of places to eat is not wide. Decide on your meals in advance. Since you're in Laguna, try or buy as gifts the specialties of neighboring Los Baños: buko pie, espasol (a cylindrical rice-flour sweet), and kesong puti (a soft white cheese).
According to recent information, the museum is open Tuesday through Sunday,
, and is closed on Mondays and public holidays. Older notices also list 8:30 a.m.–4:30 p.m. (including a midday closure), so check the NHCP museum's official Facebook page.
Admission is free. There's a donation box for upkeep, so a small contribution is welcome.
Guided explanations and video screenings are usually offered to groups that notify the museum of their visit in advance. If you want a guide, get in touch a few days beforehand.
Follow the on-site guidance on where indoor photography is allowed and on not touching the exhibits, and do not use a flash.
In your map app, search for "Rizal Shrine Calamba" or "Museo ni Jose Rizal." The entrance is on the Jose P. Rizal Street side.

The annex exhibits are in an air-conditioned building, which is a good way to cool off at midday, and they reportedly include a life-size scene of his mother Teodora telling young Rizal the story of "The Moth and the Flame."
The church and shrine are places of reverence, so modest dress is better than sleeveless tops or short shorts.
Knowing the plots of Rizal's novels "Noli Me Tangere" and "El Filibusterismo" beforehand makes the exhibits in Galleries 5 and 6 of the annex much more interesting.
SLEX gets very congested toward Manila on weekend afternoons. Time your return trip for before 3 p.m. or late in the evening.

The shrine is closed on Mondays, and may close temporarily for commemorative events or renovations. Check the latest notices before you set out, and keep in mind that there is currently no train service from Manila.

Today's house is a reconstruction of the original. Little of the original remains beyond the flooring and the well, and much of the furniture on display was arranged to match the period style, so it is often not actual Rizal family heirlooms.
The streets of the old town are narrow, with heavy car and tricycle traffic and a mix of one-way streets. Hold your child's hand firmly if you're traveling with kids.
The Calamba Crossing bus stop and the area around the malls are always busy. Keep your phone and wallet in front of you.
Fees and admission methods differ from one Pansol hot-spring resort to another. Don't settle them on the spot; confirm the reservation and rates in advance.
The garden has many dirt paths that get muddy after rain. Wear non-slip shoes.
The Calamba Baywalk is a promenade with almost no signs or monuments. There is little to see on a cloudy day, so lower your expectations when you stop by.
